# Mediator-relative routing

The two endpoints leave a deeper question: what determines whether an
intervention recruits the public route? The neutral synonym assay compares two
regimes defined by whether article identity distinguishes the intended lexical
alternatives, while keeping both alternatives semantically correct and using
the same intervention procedure. Concrete examples of the two mediator-relative
regimes are shown in @fig-routing A.

All 14 donor-derived directions pass held-out local efficacy. At native
strength, fixed-target-article target-minus-source movement is
\(0.406\ [0.281,0.604]\) logits across six between-class families and
\(0.414\ [0.297,0.555]\) across eight within-class families. Wrong-target
controls yield 0.125 and 0.008; reversed directions yield -0.385 and -0.344.
Intervention-off `a/an` policy mass averages 0.909 (minimum 0.854) and remains
0.899 after intervention. The comparison therefore clears local efficacy and
mediator-support validity without the source-initial conflict of the earlier
prompt construction.

Routing then reverses by mediator equivalence class (@fig-routing). For
between-class alternatives, every family increases the target-article policy;
mean target-article movement is 0.182 and 2/6 switch the greedy article. At
\(\tau=1\), public TV is \(0.176\ [0.108,0.243]\) and private TV is only
\(0.021\ [0.012,0.033]\). Their target-aligned effects are
\(0.189\ [0.065,0.326]\) and 0.019. For within-class alternatives, no family
switches the article and mean policy movement is 0.009. Public TV is
\(0.009\ [0.003,0.018]\), whereas private TV is
\(0.061\ [0.046,0.075]\). More importantly, public target-aligned influence is
approximately zero \(-0.001\ [-0.003,0.001]\), while private target-aligned
influence is \(0.093\ [0.062,0.124]\).

![Mediator-relative route recruitment in Gemma 3 1B. A: the article can distinguish cross-class but not same-class alternatives. B: the matched assay compares same- and cross-article targets within each of 14 semantic families; lines share a neutral prompt, source state, and source word. Diamonds and bars show means and paired-bootstrap 95% intervals. C: the initial independent-family assay provides convergent evidence.](manuscript/figures/fig_neutral_synonym_repair.png){#fig-routing width=100%}

A matched-triad test asks whether the reversal could reflect between-family
semantic composition (@fig-routing B). Fourteen neutral prompts each share the same definition,
source word, source donor, and evaluated state across one same-article and one
cross-article target; screening used only tokenization, local efficacy, and
mediator support, never route sign. At the fixed primary setting
\(\ell=17,s=1,\tau=1\), mean \(R\) changes from
\(-0.032\ [-0.057,-0.010]\) within class to
\(0.087\ [0.046,0.132]\) across classes. The paired shift is
\(0.120\ [0.077,0.161]\): 13/14 families shift in the predicted direction
(one-sided sign test \(p=0.00092\)); an exact sign-randomization test using the
paired magnitudes gives \(p=0.000122\). Eight of 14 individually show the strict
sign reversal \(R_{\rm within}<0<R_{\rm cross}\). The mean paired interaction
remains positive at all 12 tested strength--temperature settings. Thus crossing
the article mediator's equivalence boundary changes route dominance on average
while holding semantic family and source realization fixed.

Across the initial independent-family assay, public-minus-private target
influence is \(0.170\ [0.049,0.296]\) between classes, whereas
private-minus-public influence is \(0.094\ [0.060,0.126]\) within class. All six
between-class and all eight within-class families have the predicted sign
(@fig-routing C). Their between-minus-within interaction is
\(0.264\ [0.137,0.399]\), with exact family-label permutation \(p=0.00033\),
providing convergent evidence across a broader set of lexical pairs.

The result supports a precise causal statement. When article identity can
express the distinction between two correct alternatives, the intervention
recruits a target-aligned public relay. When the article maps both alternatives
to one equivalence class, token identity cannot carry their lexical difference,
and target-aligned influence persists privately. A generated token is therefore
a lossy public projection relative to the downstream distinction of interest.
We interpret the between-class effect as selective recruitment of an additional
public causal route, not conservation or transfer of a fixed information
quantity between public and private channels.
The experiment does **not** show that a natural online mechanism spontaneously
chooses a carrier: the residual direction is explicitly constructed from named
donors. The paired result identifies mediator-relative route recruitment under
controlled interventions, not a sparse endogenous routing controller.

# Closed-loop gain

Mediator visibility explains which distinctions can travel publicly, while
Equation 1 explains their gain: local pressure changes a decoder policy, and
continuation leverage determines the downstream consequence. Across 32 held-out
270M features, attribution moderately predicts local margin movement
(\(\rho=0.530\)), but attribution alone fails to predict public TV. Composing
calibrated local pressure with intervention-off decoder susceptibility and
branch leverage identifies and sizes the decisive-policy regime
(aggregate \(R^2=0.840\)); prediction among small effects is weak and crossed
feature--prompt uncertainty is wide \([-0.293,0.986]\) (@fig-gain). We therefore
claim limited predictive validation of a mechanistically coherent 270M
high-gain regime, not a universal predictor; full diagnostics are in
@fig-app-gain.

# Validity stress test at 1B

The sparse 1B campaign illustrates why the ladder's rungs cannot be collapsed:
the frozen top four are too weak, an effect-matched coalition leaves the binary
article support, and a mediator-valid frontier yields only low-amplitude hybrid
influence. Reporting only free generation would conflate these failure modes
(full table in the appendix). We use the campaign as a validity demonstration,
not evidence that scale reorganizes sparse planning mechanisms.
